title: Handling Errors
description: Use try and except to catch problems so your program keeps running.

steps.label: A line fails
steps.detail: Maybe the user typed a word, not a number.

steps.label: Python stops
steps.detail: Every line after it is skipped.

steps.label: It names the error
steps.detail: The name tells you what kind of thing went wrong.

content.title: What happens when a line fails
content.caption: An error that happens while the program runs is called an **exception**.

items.sub: IndexError: list index out of range

content.question: Which error does `int("hello")` cause?
content.explain: `"hello"` is the wrong kind of value to turn into a number, so Python raises a `ValueError`.

content.value: Catching It with try and except

content.real: A safety net under a trapeze
content.text: The acrobat (your `try` code) does the risky trick. If they slip, the net (`except`) catches them and the show goes on. If they don't slip, the net is never used.

items: Put the risky code inside a `try` block.
Something fails? Python **abandons** the rest of `try` and runs `except` instead.
Either way, the program carries on afterwards.
content.title: How it works

steps.note: Enter the `try` block. Python will watch for errors in here.
Dividing by zero fails! An exception happens, so `result` is never stored.
Python jumps straight to `except`. Line 3 is skipped: the rest of the `try` is abandoned.
No crash. The program carries on after the `try`/`except`.

content.title: Watch the jump to except
content.outro: `print(result)` never ran. The `try` block gave up at the line that failed.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `print("A")` runs, then `int("hi")` fails. Python skips the rest of `try` (so no B) and runs `except`, which prints C.

items.title: Works
items.text: Prints `5.0`. Nothing failed, so `except` is skipped.

items.title: Fails
items.text: Prints `Oops`. The division failed, so Python jumped to `except`.

content.value: Change the numbers below and watch which lines survive.

items.title: Bare except
items.text: Catches **everything**. It can't tell a typo from a divide by zero, gives one vague message, and hides bugs you'd want to know about.

items.title: Named except
items.text: Only runs for that kind of problem. You can give a clear, specific message.

items: That block only runs for that kind of error.
Python uses the **first one that matches**.
content.title: Named excepts

content.caption: Sample runs: typing `8` and `2` prints `Answer: 4.0`. Typing `8` and `zero` prints `Please type whole numbers.` Typing `8` and `0` prints `You cannot divide by zero.`

content.value: Keep the `try` block short. Only the lines that might actually fail belong inside it, so a surprise error somewhere else isn't quietly swallowed by your handler.
content.title: Keep try small

content.question: Using the code above, the user types `5` and then `0`. What prints?
content.explain: Both inputs are whole numbers, so `int()` works. Then `5 / 0` raises a `ZeroDivisionError`, which matches the second `except`.

items: Catching an error is most useful when you **do something** about it.
Put the `try` inside a loop to keep asking until the answer makes sense.
`break` only runs if the risky line worked.
A failure jumps to `except` and never reaches `break`, so the loop goes round again.
content.title: Retry loop

steps.note: Start a loop that would go on forever, unless something breaks out.
The user types `ten`. `int("ten")` fails with a `ValueError`.
Python jumps to the matching `except`. The `break` on line 4 is skipped.
Tell the user what went wrong.
out: Whole numbers only, please. Try again.

steps.note: Back round the loop. This time the user types `10`, and `int` works.
No error, so Python reaches `break` and leaves the loop.
The program carries on with a good value.

content.title: A bad answer, then a good one
content.outro: That's the difference between a program that crashes on a typo and one that simply asks again.

content.question: In the retry loop, why does `break` only run when the input is valid?
content.explain: When the risky line fails, Python abandons the rest of `try`, including `break`, and runs `except`. So the loop repeats.

practice.question: Wrap the division in a try/except so a zero denominator prints 'Division failed!' instead of crashing.
practice.starterCode:
numerator = 10
denominator = 0

# Put the division inside a try block, and print 'Division failed!' in the except
result = numerator / denominator
print(result)

practice.question: This catches everything with a bare except. Change it to catch only ValueError.

quiz.question: Which block holds the code that might cause an error?
quiz.explain: The try block holds the risky lines. If one of them fails, the except block underneath runs instead.

quiz.question: What happens if the code in a try block works with no errors?
options: The try block runs a second time
quiz.explain: There is no error to catch, so the except block is skipped completely and the program carries on below it.

quiz.question: In this code, what is printed?  try:  /  print("A")  /  print(10 / 0)  /  print("B")  /  except:  /  print("C")
quiz.explain: A prints, then the division fails, so the rest of the try block is abandoned. B never runs and Python jumps straight to C.
